speakers: Steve Eisman (host, The Real Eisman Playbook)
summary: Eisman interviews Evercore's Krishna Guha on Fed chair Walsh's rate hike, QE and balance sheet views, forward guidance, and Bessent's Treasury buybacks. Guha attributes the 10-year at ~5.25% to AI/government issuance, higher neutral rate and oil, not Walsh. Main risk: stocks and consumer wealth effect at 5%+ yields.

coverage.note: Why Walsh hiked; inflation outlook; insurance hike
Walsh supply-side view; QE debate (wealth effect, Eisman skeptic)
QE cost-of-capital channel; Walsh on QE/balance sheet; 10y yield move
Causes of yield rise: issuance, r-star, oil/diesel, Fed uncertainty
History and value of forward guidance; sponsor read (Arca) excluded
Strong vs broad guidance; guard rails removed; Bessent intro
Bessent buybacks/operation twist, size, two-sided risk
Bank liquidity regulation, issuance signal, credibility, AI rate sensitivity
Rate sensitivity AI vs non-AI, housing, wealth effect risk; Greenspan intro
Fed chair ratings: Greenspan, Bernanke, Yellen
Powell: COVID backstop, inflation lag, soft landing, tariffs

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: you worry that people are going to start to just expect higher inflation and then factor that in to their wage negotiations the prices that businesses large and small set in a way that can lock it into the system
claims.claim: After inflation has been above target for 5+ years, a central bank can no longer look through supply shocks because rising inflation expectations feed wages and prices and become self-locking, which justifies a hike.
claims.indicator: Inflation above 2% target for >5 years; inflation expectations
claims.direction: Fed hikes; tighter policy when expectations risk de-anchoring
claims.conditions: When shocks (tariffs, oil) are persistent and labor market is sound
claims.testable: partly - needs an expectations series and a duration-above-target rule

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: I do think that the tariff inflation is going to drop into, you know, drop out of the numbers fairly soon.
claims.claim: Guha expects inflation to keep falling because the tariff price-level effect rolls out of year-over-year data and oil is not seen creating a lasting impulse.
claims.conditions: If oil does not create a lasting inflation impulse
claims.testable: no - a forecast about one episode

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: the fact that the labor market, the jobs market is in pretty good shape is telling you that maybe it's a good time to take out some insurance on the inflation side.
claims.claim: A healthy labor market gives a central bank room to hike pre-emptively as insurance against inflation without much risk to growth.
claims.conditions: Labor market in good shape; inflation data improving
claims.testable: partly - can test hikes when unemployment is low versus later growth

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: Kevin Walsh sees himself more as a supply cider, more in that sort of small C conservative economist tradition.
claims.claim: A Fed chair who frames the economy as driven by supply (productivity, labor incentives) rather than demand will rely on different models and may run policy differently from the new-Keynesian consensus of the past 20 years.
claims.conditions: Depends on how the chair actually acts versus rhetoric
claims.testable: no - regime of ideas, hard to quantify

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: Now, of course, that is working in part by pushing up the value of assets, creating wealth gains that then support consumer spending, right?
claims.claim: QE supports demand by raising asset values, which create wealth effects that lift consumer spending.
claims.conditions: Most effective when policy rate is at zero and demand is weak
claims.testable: partly - QE episodes studied in event-time

claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.quote: quantitative easing did absolutely nothing to help the actual economy, but inflated asset prices
claims.claim: Eisman holds that QE lifted asset prices without helping the real economy, in contrast to the view that it worked through wealth and cost-of-capital channels.
claims.testable: partly - disputed in the same conversation

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: Because a company's borrowing rate will be the government's borrowing rate plus some kind of spread.
claims.claim: QE lowers government yields, and since corporate borrowing costs are government yields plus a spread, it also lowers corporate cost of capital and supports investment and hiring.
claims.direction: corporate borrowing costs down, investment up
claims.conditions: Spreads must not widen enough to offset
claims.testable: yes - decompose corporate yields into Treasury and spread around QE

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: He actually agrees that there is a role for QE when markets seize up.
claims.claim: Walsh accepts QE only as an emergency tool when markets seize up, and opposes continued QE to strengthen growth because it adds little at high cost in balance sheet size and asset prices.
claims.conditions: Market dysfunction events such as financial crisis or early pandemic

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: if he just announces tomorrow that he's going to dump a whole load of Treasury bonds and mortgage bonds into the market, he will drive long-term interest rates to the sky.
claims.claim: Shrinking the Fed balance sheet abruptly would push long-term yields sharply higher, so balance-sheet reduction has to be gradual.
claims.indicator: Fed holdings of Treasuries and MBS; long yields
claims.conditions: Especially when long yields are already rising
claims.testable: yes - QT announcement and pace versus term premium

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: I think he's going to look for a window of opportunity when bond market conditions stabilize, when yields come down some
claims.claim: Guha expects Walsh to wait for stable bond markets and lower yields before restarting a plan to shrink the balance sheet gradually.
claims.conditions: Bond yields stabilize or fall
claims.testable: no - a forecast about one person

claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.quote: it's five and a quarter now
claims.claim: The 10-year Treasury yield rose from about 4.5% in July to about 5.25% at the time of recording, a very large move.

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: there are more borrowers competing for savings competing for capital and so that's bidding up the the the rate they have to pay.
claims.claim: Heavy debt issuance by AI hyperscalers on top of a government deficit near 6% of GDP means more borrowers compete for a given pool of savings, pushing yields up (private sector crowding out government).
claims.indicator: Corporate and government bond issuance; deficit at 6% of GDP
claims.conditions: Savings pool limited
claims.testable: partly - issuance volumes versus term premium

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: saying we've moved from a world where there was too much saving chasing too few investment opportunities to a world in which there's a huge demand to invest chasing a limited pool of savings
claims.claim: A multi-year AI investment boom raises the neutral rate (r-star) because investment demand now exceeds savings, so the normal Fed funds rate over the next several years should be higher.
claims.conditions: Persistence of the AI capex boom

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: Is putting upward pressure on inflation and on bond yields.
claims.claim: A renewed oil rise after the US-Iran ceasefire broke down pushes up inflation and bond yields.
claims.direction: oil up, inflation up, yields up
claims.conditions: Persistent supply disruption in the Middle East
claims.testable: yes - oil changes versus yield changes

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: you're not getting the full picture because refined product like diesel and jet fuel has actually increased a lot more than you would think
claims.claim: Crude or gasoline prices understate the energy shock because refined products such as diesel and jet fuel rose much more (diesel roughly doubled, comparable to oil near 200 dollars).
claims.indicator: Diesel and jet fuel prices versus WTI/Brent
claims.conditions: Refined product tightness
claims.testable: yes - diesel crack and price series

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: bond investors looking at the Fed and saying, you know, how far are they planning to go with these rate hikes?
claims.claim: Uncertainty over how far the Fed will hike, with no stated roadmap, adds to upward pressure on bond yields.
claims.conditions: When the central bank gives little explanation
claims.testable: partly - proxies for policy uncertainty exist

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: policy also works better when the markets in particular and also the public understand what the central bank's trying to do
claims.claim: Central-bank communication about its reaction function (what it watches and how it would respond) makes policy more effective and lets businesses plan, which is why consensus moved to more guidance over 30 years.
claims.conditions: Normal times and stress alike
claims.testable: partly - guidance regimes compared in event studies

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: a central bank shouldn't project or communicate more confidence about the future than it than than than it really has
claims.claim: Strong forward guidance (firm commitments to hike a set number of times) is risky because the world is uncertain and the bank can get locked into wrong actions, so it should be an emergency tool only.
claims.conditions: Crises (pandemic, financial crisis) versus normal times
claims.testable: partly - compare guided versus unguided cycles

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: Worshes removed those guard rails and that has contributed in my view to rates markets
claims.claim: Removing general forward guidance leaves bond markets guessing the Fed's criteria, so repricings overshoot; Guha says the main yield drivers are AI, issuance, war and oil but lack of guidance amplified the move.
claims.direction: yield volatility up; long yields up
claims.conditions: When fundamentals are already shifting
claims.testable: partly - rates volatility around communication changes

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: you're buying the long stuff, issuing the short stuff, and the idea is it'll bring down the long-term rates.
claims.claim: Treasury buybacks of long bonds funded with bills work as an operation twist that aims to lower long-term yields.
claims.conditions: Scale must be large relative to the market

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: it can be efficient for the treasury to buy back those bonds and then issue the kind of bonds that people actually want to hold.
claims.claim: Buying back old illiquid bonds with low prices and high yields is efficient for the Treasury but has little overall effect on yields.

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: you've absolutely brought a knife to a gunfight
claims.claim: A buyback of a few billion dollars is too small to stabilize a roughly 40 trillion dollar Treasury market, so ramping it as a yield-capping tool fails.
claims.indicator: Buyback size versus Treasury market size
claims.conditions: Fails when size is tiny relative to the market

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: create some two-sided risk in the mind of particularly leveraged uh investors
claims.claim: Buyback announcements can create two-sided risk for leveraged investors so hedge funds do not hold a one-way short in Treasuries, which may prevent overshooting.
claims.conditions: Works only if the intervention is credible

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: reforming regulations in a way that in effect um encourages banks to hold fewer Fed reserves
claims.claim: Reforming bank liquidity rules such as the LCR so banks hold fewer reserves and more Treasuries (probably bills) could add demand for government debt and help shrink the Fed balance sheet.
claims.indicator: Liquidity coverage ratio; bank Treasury holdings; Fed reserves
claims.direction: bank Treasury demand up, reserves down
claims.conditions: Regulatory change must pass

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: future government debt issuance may be shifted from these longerterm bonds to the shorter duration bonds.
claims.claim: A shift in Treasury issuance toward bills signals less long-bond supply and can affect long yields today.
claims.direction: long yields down; bill supply up
claims.conditions: Credibility of the signal

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: serious governments like the US government tend not to intervene in their own debt market
claims.claim: Intervening in the home debt market signals difficulty selling debt, a pattern typical of struggling emerging markets, and so can hurt confidence and raise yields on net.
claims.indicator: US Treasury yields after buyback announcement
claims.conditions: Credibility issues

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: The AI story is plausibly a lot less interest rate sensitive than other types of normal business activity.
claims.claim: AI investment and wealth effects make the US economy in aggregate less sensitive to higher rates than before the AI boom, which makes it hard to pinpoint the yield level where growth slows.
claims.indicator: Aggregate interest rate sensitivity; AI capex
claims.conditions: Until a breaking point in rates or equity prices
claims.testable: partly - rate sensitivity estimates by sector

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: with a five handle which is putting strain on the nonAI uh parts of the economy
claims.claim: With 10-year yields above 5% the non-AI economy faces crowding out because borrowing costs are too high for ordinary businesses (the AI half is insensitive when expected returns are huge).
claims.conditions: Applies to non-AI firms and small businesses

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: Housing is completely bombed out because mortgage rates are 7%.
claims.claim: Housing is the first sector to take the strain from higher long yields because mortgage rates near 7% have crushed activity.
claims.conditions: Mortgage rates around 7%
claims.testable: yes - housing starts and sales versus mortgage rates

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: that might require rates to go long-term borrowing costs to go even significantly higher from here say six handle or something
claims.claim: AI investment itself would only be clearly impaired if long-term borrowing costs rose significantly further (a 6% handle on the 10-year), but AI stock gains may come under pressure earlier.
claims.direction: AI capex down; AI stocks down
claims.conditions: Threshold is a guess

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: The AI investment spend a lot of it actually goes on imports.
claims.claim: AI capex leaks abroad through imported chips while consumption funded by stock wealth is spent at home, so a stock sell-off hits domestic demand more than AI investment suggests.

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: whether the stock market can withstand, you know, 10-year yields in this zip code because if the stock market sells off, then you have a wealth problem
claims.claim: Consumer spending is being held up by wealth gains at the top, so the key risk is whether equities can tolerate 10-year yields near 5.25%; a sell-off would hit the consumer through a negative wealth effect.
claims.indicator: S&P 500 versus 10-year yield; wealth effect on consumption
claims.conditions: Consumer already squeezed by wages and gasoline

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: contributed importantly to the lack of of you know of financial stability regulation that we ultimately paid a very heavy price for in the financial crisis
claims.claim: Greenspan's belief that markets are self-equilibrating helped produce weak financial stability regulation that was paid for in the financial crisis, even though his macro management was rated very good.

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: It was the ban tools that were pulled out the cupboard to deal with co
claims.claim: The crisis toolkit built by Bernanke (market backstops, QE, forward guidance) was reused in the pandemic, so central banks can reliably stabilize seized markets with the same tools.
claims.conditions: When markets seize up

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: the Fed needed to keep rates uh very low for much longer than many people thought in order to try to foster a fuller labor market recovery.
claims.claim: Keeping policy rates low for longer than expected after the financial crisis fostered a fuller labor-market recovery, because structural issues held back the economy.
claims.indicator: Fed funds rate; labor market slack
claims.conditions: Deep structural drag after a financial crisis

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: he was willing to effectively backs stop private sector borrowing, not just government bonds
claims.claim: An aggressive backstop of private-sector borrowing in March 2020 prevented a 2008-scale financial crisis.
claims.conditions: In a liquidity seizure
claims.testable: partly - spreads before and after announcements

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: the Fed was slow to grasp the strength and persistence of inflation after the pandemic and then had to play catchup.
claims.claim: After a large demand and supply shock the Fed was slow to recognize persistent inflation, then hiked fast to catch up.
claims.conditions: After pandemic stimulus and supply disruption

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: bring inflation down without pushing unemployment up by any meaningful amount
claims.claim: Rapid 2022 hikes plus QE shutdown achieved a soft landing that most economists thought unreachable, contrary to recession consensus.

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: launches a trade war, which of course uh creates at least an initial wave of inflation because imported prices shoot up
claims.claim: A tariff trade war produces an initial wave of inflation through higher import prices.

claims.speaker: Krishna Guha
claims.quote: tariff impact is starting to roll over, we have the war, we have a shooting war in the Middle East and we have oil shooting up
claims.claim: Successive shocks (tariffs rolling over, then the Middle East war and oil spike, then the AI demand boom) prevented inflation from completing its final move back to 2%.

claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.quote: they simply move with oil prices and the yield on the 10-year
claims.claim: Eisman observes that daily equity market moves are driven by oil prices and the 10-year yield.
claims.direction: stocks down when oil or yields up
claims.conditions: Current regime
claims.testable: yes - rolling correlations of S&P with oil and 10-year
